Saving micro babies

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Premature babies born before 25 weeks are called micro prems and have almost no chance of survival outside the womb. Find out how doctors are working to save these tiny babies.

Summary:
Premature babies born sub 25 weeks – are known as micro prems – and some neonatal units in South Africa have developed such advanced bio mimicry incubators – in other words an extra uterine womb as close to nature as possible – that these minute babies are given more than a fighting chance.

Dr. Ricky Dipenaar is a neonatologist and he heads up units at Cape Towns Blouberg and N1 City Netcare hospitals where he specialises in the care of these tiny babies. All babies born before the 40-week gestation period are considered premature, but these sub 25-weekers are far more high risk because their organs and systems are not fully developed.

Dr Dipenaar and his team create extra uterine incubators to help these babies survive. From using ziplock bags or velcro bags, an artificial womb is created for these tiny babies. Micro-prems are so small that they can fit in the palm of your hand and they have very translucent skin. Their arms and veins are too small for an intravenous line so their feeding line is connected to their umbilicus and that's how they get their nutrition.

A humidifier is then used to correct the temperature in the artificial womb and that's where the babies spend the first few weeks until they're "full term" babies and ready to go home.

Further information:
Not all micro babies are viable for this procedure and in most cases, there are a number of factors which determine whether doctors can try and save the baby.

One of the mothers that we meet had been trying to have a baby for a few years and was going through fertility treatments. Her twin boys were born at 24 weeks and were incubated in artificial wombs. Unfortunately the stronger twin - the more viable twin - died 17 days after. Joshua, trumped as the weaker twin was born weighing 500g - half a kilogram of sugar, and he manged to survive. Joshua is now four years old.

Allegra Lategan spent the first few weeks of her life in 2011 in a ziplock bag to protect her paper-thin skin from tearing against the sheets and to prevent heat loss from her fragile body. She was born at 22 weeks and weighed only 515 grams. Allegra was expected to be a prem baby and she was delivered naturally and placed in a Ziplock bag.

Zanele Dwane didn't know that she was 22 weeks pregnant and after doctors realised that her baby was in distress, they tried to keep him in the womb for a little longer. But three weeks later baby Ntikelelo was delivered by C- section.

Press Release:


Babies born prematurely at less than 28 weeks have underdeveloped organs and a very slim chance of survival. But even with the odds stacked against them, neonatologists have found novel ways to save these little lives. Carte Blanche witnesses how an ordinary plastic sandwich bag is miraculously transformed into a temporary artificial womb in which micro babies can grow.

Script:


Script
UPSOUND Amanda Rohner:
We went for our twenty week scan, it’s the big important scan. Everything was perfectly fine. And something must have happened at week 23.

UPSOUND Chantal Lategan:
I stood up one morning to get ready for work, and my water broke. At that stage, I didn’t even realize what was going on. I just knew something was wrong.

UPSOUND Zanele Zibi:
They told me that the cord that’s holding the baby is torn apart so if they keep the baby longer in the tummy then the cord might be totally torn off then the baby might die.

VO: It’s perhaps every pregnant woman’s worst nightmare coming true.

Just over 20 weeks into your pregnancy and your doctor tells you, you’ve got to deliver.

UPSOUND Prof Smith:
The problem with prematurity in South Africa is our rates are higher, three to four times higher than first world countries.

50% of moms will just go into premature labour and deliver the baby for reasons, we never seem to quite get to the root of the problem.


VO: Baby Dominique Dreyer is just ten days old but he’s already been in the fight for his life.

He had a heart problem and had to be delivered at 27 weeks and two days, weighing 650 grams.

He’s what neonatologists describe as a micro baby.
UPSOUND Prof Smith:
A micro baby is any baby weighing less than 1000grams, 1Kg and if we talk in terms of gestational age, then we talk of equal or less than 28 weeks.


VO: VO: At this stage of pregnancy, the foetus is about the size of a cauliflower.

The brain cells are still developing, the lungs are immature and the baby’s skin is very fragile.

A baby born this prematurely is a high risk delivery and according to Professor Johan Smith, the Head of Neonatology at Tygerberg Hospital, in many cases the baby would not make it.

UPSOUND Prof Smith:
In South Africa, 27, 28 weeks would be regarded as the limit of viability.
In this type of setting anything between 25 – 45 %of them will not survive but when they die, they die within the first 48 – 72 hours.

UPSOUND Chantal Lategan:
… When she was born that night, I will never forget, the nurse that was there had to fill in forms and she said according to the forms it was a miscarriage.

LINK
In 2011, Allegre Lategan was born in this hospital at 22 weeks, weighing just 515 gram.

VO: Chantal Lategan and her husband Hennie, had already experienced the devastation of a miscarriage but when their little girl was born too early, her doctor warned them of her slim chances of survival.

UPSOUND Chantal Lategan:
He came to us and said her chances of survival is about 5 percent if that at all. He said she had bleeding on the brain, her lungs were completely undeveloped, as well as her other organs.

VO: Dr Ricky Dippenaar was the consulting neonatologist on the case at Blaauberg Hospital and he and his team decided to use an unusual method to try and save Allegre’s life – the humble ziplock bag.

UPSOUND Dr DIP:
The ziplock bag or any plastic has been used in teaching for advanced life support for many years already.
The problem is that in Allegra’s case which was our first experience with it we had, we needed to buy time so we had to think slightly outside of the box.

UPSOUND Prof Smith:
A ziplock bag or a sort of cling wrap we use to wrap these little ones when they are born. They are obviously born wet and it’s a cold environment, so you wrap them into these little plastic sheets and bags and then they maintain their body temperature.
VO: Amanda Rohner and her husband Robert, turned to in vitro fertilisation after struggling for years to have a baby.

Amanda fell pregnant with twins, but just 23 weeks into the pregnancy, her babies were in trouble.

UPSOUND Amanda Rohner:
We landed up going to the ER. That’s when we sort of got the news that I was 5cm dilated and both heads were down... it was actually almost a week later, I gave birth.

VO: And for the new mom, seeing her twin boys for the first time wrapped in plastic, was a traumatic experience.

UPSPOUND Amanda Rohner:
Oh John, I didn’t expect it. I remember, I think Caleb had the little beanie on, knitted beanie. And Joshua was just, no beanie. [01:37:54] … They had their little plastic covers – or ziplock bags, as Dr Dippenaar would call it. Ja, and they were just lying there… they looked lifeless.

UPSOUND Dr DIP:
It seemed a logical first step to buy us time and it worked absolutely brilliantly. The ziplock bag was a good solution to a challenging problem.

VO: But this isn’t the only challenge facing doctors and nurses.

Micro babies have incredibly sensitive skin which can be torn even by harmless materials like bed sheets, so the plastic covers give them added protection.

UPSOUND Prof Smith:
Anything you stick onto these little ones skins, you have to remove it very cautiously with specific solutions otherwise and even if you’re cautious you may still peel off the superficial layer of the skin and sometimes deeper.

VO: Chantal and Morne Coetzee’s little boy Hattighe, spent many long hours with a breathing mask plastered to his face.

UPSOUND Chantal Coetzee: The plasters that they put on and off his face every day, I was worried about the scars that would be left behind on his cheeks.

VO: At birth micro babies are unable to breast feed and miss out on vital nutrition from breast milk.
So a small surgical procedure is performed to connect an umbilical canulis, to the blood vessels that are in the umbilical stump.

UPSOUND Dr DIP:
… we connect into the artery and into the vein and through that we can monitor blood. We can take blood can provide nutrition we can affect and alter the electro lights solutions.

LINK
In normal births, hearing and eyesight are monitored very closely and tested almost immediately but in babies born under 1000 grams, those two things are evaluated even more closely.

UPSOUND Dr DIP:
The eyes are particularly sensitive to oxygen if you interrupt the growth of the retina then you have the potential to be blind so we have to monitor those eyes because we can intervene.

UPSOUND Zanele Zibi:
First of all I didn’t know I was pregnant until a week before. So when I found and went to the gynae, the gynae told me I was 25 weeks pregnant.

VO: Zanele Zibi gave birth to her son Ntsikelelo just a week after she found out that she was pregnant. For months it remained unclear whether he could hear.

UPSOUND Zanele Zibi:
When he did the first test, he failed the test, the doc said it’s probably because he is still tiny. There’s a lot of liquid in his ears because not a lot of things have developed yet.
He also failed the second test, and I was a bit worried now.

UPSOUND Dr Ricky DIP:
Hearing is a tricky one... the impact is variable. We don’t quite know what is triggering it certain drugs can trigger it and simply pre maturity can trigger it.

UPSOUND Zanele Zibi:
I was really certain, I was very sure that he is deaf, he can’t hear. We went for another one recently and that one was much better than the first ones and now he responds well.

VO: But the Lategans were in for difficult news. Multiple tests showed that Allegra would face significant challenges.

UPSOUND TCR: 02:26:47:00 HENNIE: … we had her eyes and ears tested but because she was so small it was difficult to tell whether they were working or not.
.…then they said to us she has hearing loss in both ears – a lot of hearing loss. It was before her second birthday that she got her hearing implant.

VO: Despite these challenges however, Allegra continues to grow from strength to strength.

JW: Wie se naam is dit?

Allegra: Allegra
LINK
Many micro babies are born smaller than my hand with organs that are yet to fully develop, it’s under those circumstances that parents often find it quite difficult to make an immediate connection.

UPSOUND Zanele Zibi
I cried the first time and I just went out because I didn’t want to see him. It was really traumatic for me.

UPSOUND [01:38:37] Amanda Rohner: For me, they just didn’t look ‘normal’. The skin was red, they were lifeless, they were in bags...I didn’t expect that. I wasn’t prepared for this.

VO: After a period of time inside these plastic covers, the baby is then fully supported by a specialised machine called the Giraffe Incubator.

But for baby Caleb, the older and stronger of the Rohner twins, this wasn’t enough and just 17 days later, he passed away.

UPSOUND [01:42:00] Amanda: ...there’s always a chance when the one passed away, when Caleb passed away, in the back of your mind you always think, is it a matter of time and Joshua’s going to go down that same road?

VO: But, he didn’t. Joshua is now a thriving four year-old.

LINK: Tragically not all unborn distressed micro babies can be saved in this way but a combination of modern medicine and great doctors and nurses are at the very least giving many others a fighting chance.

UPSOUND Prof Smith
I can say with our experience that 75% of our babies survive and 70 % more or less of them more or less will have intact or very good survival.

VO: Back at Blaauberg hospital in the maternity ward, baby Hattighe Coetzee who’s spent the first 100 days of his life in Intensive Care, is finally going home.

UPSOUND John Webb: So today is the day that you leave? How are you feeling.

UPSOUND CHANTAL Coetzee: Sjoh! Very overwhelmed, emotional.
Really, as I said, I never thought the day would come.
One thing is, I don’t know how to say thank you to the medical staff, because they gave us our
child, they gave us a son.

UPSOUND Prof Smith I can say with our experience that 75% of our babies survive and 70 % more or less of them more or less will have intact or very good survival. VO: Back at Blaauberg hospital in the maternity ward, baby Hattighe Coetzee who’s spent the first 100 days of his life in Intensive Care, is finally going home. UPSOUND John Webb: So today is the day that you leave? How are you feeling. UPSOUND CHANTAL Coetzee: Sjoh! Very overwhelmed, emotional. Really, as I said, I never thought the day would come. One thing is, I don’t know how to say thank you to the medical staff, because they gave us our child, they gave us a son.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Premature babies born before 25 weeks are called micro prems and have almost no chance of survival outside the womb. Find out how doctors are working to save these tiny babies.
metadata.Summary: Premature babies born sub 25 weeks – are known as micro prems – and some neonatal units in South Africa have developed such advanced bio mimicry incubators – in other words an extra uterine womb as close to nature as possible – that these minute babies are given more than a fighting chance. Dr. Ricky Dipenaar is a neonatologist and he heads up units at Cape Towns Blouberg and N1 City Netcare hospitals where he specialises in the care of these tiny babies. All babies born before the 40-week gestation period are considered premature, but these sub 25-weekers are far more high risk because their organs and systems are not fully developed. Dr Dipenaar and his team create extra uterine incubators to help these babies survive. From using ziplock bags or velcro bags, an artificial womb is created for these tiny babies. Micro-prems are so small that they can fit in the palm of your hand and they have very translucent skin. Their arms and veins are too small for an intravenous line so their feeding line is connected to their umbilicus and that's how they get their nutrition. A humidifier is then used to correct the temperature in the artificial womb and that's where the babies spend the first few weeks until they're "full term" babies and ready to go home.
metadata.Further information: Not all micro babies are viable for this procedure and in most cases, there are a number of factors which determine whether doctors can try and save the baby. One of the mothers that we meet had been trying to have a baby for a few years and was going through fertility treatments. Her twin boys were born at 24 weeks and were incubated in artificial wombs. Unfortunately the stronger twin - the more viable twin - died 17 days after. Joshua, trumped as the weaker twin was born weighing 500g - half a kilogram of sugar, and he manged to survive. Joshua is now four years old. Allegra Lategan spent the first few weeks of her life in 2011 in a ziplock bag to protect her paper-thin skin from tearing against the sheets and to prevent heat loss from her fragile body. She was born at 22 weeks and weighed only 515 grams. Allegra was expected to be a prem baby and she was delivered naturally and placed in a Ziplock bag. Zanele Dwane didn't know that she was 22 weeks pregnant and after doctors realised that her baby was in distress, they tried to keep him in the womb for a little longer. But three weeks later baby Ntikelelo was delivered by C- section.
